store.0: I’ve been dabbling in undergrad research since the end of my sophomore year, and honestly, it’s been one of the most eye-opening parts of my college experience. It’s given me this glimpse into how knowledge is actually created in the tech world, and it’s pretty cool to be part of that. Back when I was a freshman, I didn’t really see myself going down the research route. I mean, I was into coding projects, hackathons, stuff like that, but I never thought of research as something that was, I don’t know, ‘my thing.’ But then one of my professors—she taught an introductory data science class—told me there was an opening for a research assistant in a lab focused on data visualization for big scientific datasets. She saw I had a knack for bridging technical coding with a sense of user experience. At first, I was hesitant because research sounded intimidating. But I took the leap, and it turned out to be a great decision.
store.1: The lab I’m in is this interdisciplinary space where computer scientists partner with scientists from all sorts of backgrounds—astronomy, environmental science, even neuroscience—to figure out how we can make massive amounts of data more comprehensible. You know how in classes you’ll sometimes do small data projects or maybe tackle a 1GB dataset for a machine learning project? Well, in our lab, we deal with datasets that are tens of terabytes in size. Trying to visualize that so that a domain expert(like an astrophysicist) can quickly glean insights is no joke. So one of my main tasks is working on front-end prototypes that take slices of data and present them in dynamic, interactive dashboards. It’s a combination of advanced JavaScript frameworks, a bit of D3.js for custom visualizations, and sometimes specialized libraries for volumetric rendering if we’re dealing with 3D data.
store.2: The first research project I really got into was about visualizing oceanic temperature changes over time for a climate study group. They had these daily temperature readings from buoys all around the Pacific. The raw data was enormous—like, tons of files scattered across different servers, each representing a single day’s worth of readings at tiny intervals. Our job was to aggregate and present them in a coherent way that could show patterns over months or even years. I dove in headfirst: writing scripts to clean and unify the data, building a pipeline that could handle near real-time updates, and then designing interfaces that let researchers zoom into a particular region or timeframe. Eventually, I co-authored my first paper on this system. I’m not going to lie, I freaked out a bit when I saw my name in an official publication—it felt so surreal, and it’s probably one of my proudest moments in college.
store.3: These days, my research has pivoted to something slightly different but still under the umbrella of data visualization: specifically, I’m working on immersive analytics platforms. Essentially, we’re exploring how VR or AR technologies might help scientists get an even more intuitive feel for complex data. If you think about it, looking at raw numerical data in a spreadsheet is one thing, and 2D visuals(like graphs) are another step up. But actually being able to walk around a 3D representation of data in a virtual environment—touch it, rotate it, highlight subsets—might be a game-changer for some fields. It’s definitely a leap from just coding up websites. There’s a lot of experimentation, plugging in VR headsets, integrating with engines like Unity or Unreal, and figuring out how to efficiently stream data into a 3D environment. It’s all super cutting-edge, but that’s what makes it fun. Every day, you’re forging your own path because there isn’t a huge, established best-practice library for VR data visualization just yet.
store.4: Now, let me talk about the nitty-gritty of research life. A lot of people imagine it as me sitting in a quiet corner coding away at some mysterious project, but actually, it’s a lot of reading. Like, academic papers never end. If I’m trying to solve a bug with how to render certain volumetric data in VR, there’s a good chance someone has tried something similar, wrote about it in a conference proceeding or workshop, and I need to comb through it. It can get overwhelming, but over time, you learn how to skim effectively—looking at the abstract, introduction, and conclusion to see if a paper’s relevant before diving into all the details. Occasionally, when I discover something interesting, I’ll share it with the rest of the lab, and we’ll discuss how we can incorporate that technique into our own workflow.
store.5: I also get to interact with a bunch of graduate students—both master's and PhD. That’s a bit intimidating at first, because they’re so deeply immersed in their niche fields, but it’s also inspiring. There’s this one PhD student in our lab who’s been developing a machine learning algorithm to do on-the-fly compression of large datasets, and he’s trying to integrate it with our VR platform. So essentially, the idea is that if you’re looking at a huge climate dataset, you don’t need to have every single point fully loaded at once in VR—a compressed representation might be enough until you zoom in. It’s wild, but super practical for real-time performance. Working alongside him means I get to see how advanced theoretical concepts actually get applied. Some of our best brainstorming sessions happen spontaneously—like in the lab break room, sipping coffee and hashing out how we can offload some processing to the GPU.
store.6: We’ve also done a few poster presentations at smaller symposiums around campus, which was a great experience. You have to boil down complex research into easy-to-digest visuals and talking points. The first time I presented, I was sweating bullets. The idea of random professors or industry folks walking by, asking tough questions, really freaked me out. But it turned out to be more like a friendly dialogue. People are genuinely interested in what you’re doing. There were even a few folks from local startups who showed up, and they had some interesting perspectives on how VR for data visualization could benefit commercial industries—like marketing analytics or even architecture. It opened my eyes to how research can transition from academia to real-world applications.
store.7: As for publications, I’ve been lucky enough to be a co-author on two workshop papers and I’m currently working on a larger conference submission. The bigger conference is the IEEE Visualization Conference(commonly known as IEEE VIS), which is a pretty big deal in our area. We’re focusing on a user study that compares traditional 2D dashboards with an interactive VR environment. Our hypothesis is that VR immersion helps researchers spot anomalies or trends faster than they would with just a plain old 2D chart. We ran a small set of user trials—like 15 participants—recorded their times, asked them to fill out a UX questionnaire, all that jazz. Now we’re crunching the data to see if there’s a statistically significant difference. Writing the paper is a group effort: I’m handling the sections on system architecture and prototype design, someone else is writing about the user study methodology, and our PI(principal investigator) is weaving it all into a cohesive narrative. It’s definitely a balancing act, especially since I have my senior coursework and a capstone project to manage.
store.8: Sometimes I get asked if I plan on going to grad school myself. Right now, I’m leaning toward working in the industry for a couple of years—hopefully at a tech company that values R&D or advanced solution building—before deciding if I want to pursue a master’s or PhD. The idea of contributing to cutting-edge knowledge is really tempting, especially in areas like data visualization or machine learning. But I also want to see how these concepts get applied in real product development. One of my mentors in the lab said that sometimes stepping into industry can give you a better perspective on what problems are truly relevant, so that if you do come back for a PhD, you’ll have a more practical approach.
store.9: Oh, and I’d be lying if I said it’s all been sunshine and rainbows. Research can be frustrating. You’ll spend weeks on an approach that doesn’t pan out, or you’ll discover your entire idea has already been done—and improved upon—by a group in Europe or somewhere else. That part can feel like a punch in the gut. But the key is to adapt. We’ll read that existing paper, incorporate their findings, either think of a new angle or a new application, and push the boundary. That’s the essence of research. You’re never truly starting from scratch; you’re building on this giant foundation of what others have done. The sense of collaboration—both within our lab and among the global research community—is something I find really special.
store.10: One story that really stands out: a few months ago, one of our massive servers crashed. We had vital data stored there—some of which wasn’t fully backed up(I know, rookie mistake, but we learned from it). I remember the scramble that night: a frantic email chain, Zoom calls with the lab manager, everyone trying to see if we could recover the data. We did manage to restore most of it, but that crisis hammered home the importance of data backups. After that fiasco, we set up a better backup system, plus some checks to ensure we never again rely on a single point of failure. It was stressful, but also kind of a bonding experience for the whole lab.
store.11: Another big plus is that research connects me with professors on a more personal level than just being a face in the lecture hall. My PI is super approachable; if I have a question about the direction of my career or even something I’m struggling with in class, I know I can pop into her office and chat. She’s been recommending me for different scholarships, events, and networking opportunities. I got to attend a virtual workshop on immersive analytics that was filled with academic experts from all around the world. Getting to see them debate technical details, propose new frameworks, and even gently tease each other over rival theories was fascinating. It was like I was witnessing the frontier of CS knowledge in real time.
store.12: So yeah, that’s basically my journey in the research world so far. It’s a lot of work, often more chaotic than you’d expect, but also super rewarding. I love the feeling that what I do in the lab might end up shaping the way scientists understand their data five or ten years down the line. Maybe one day the VR and immersive stuff we’re trying to pioneer will become standard tools, and I’ll be able to look back and say, ‘Hey, I was part of that from the beginning.’ It’s that sense of contributing to something bigger that really keeps me motivated. Whether or not I go to grad school soon, I know this experience has changed how I think about computer science, about innovation, and even about teamwork. I can’t imagine my undergrad years without it—it’s definitely enriched my whole perspective on what it means to be a computer scientist.
